$$|a|\leq\frac{w}{2(m^2-1)}.$$
For completeness this condition is also sufficient here. Define the periodic curve $X=hn+h^{\prime} t$, so $X^{\prime}=\rho t$. For any fixed $\alpha$ and $\theta\in[\alpha,\alpha+\pi]$,
$$(X(\theta)-X(\alpha))\cdot n(\alpha)=\int_\alpha^\theta\rho(s)\sin(\alpha-s)\,ds\leq0.$$
For $\theta\in[\alpha+\pi,\alpha+2\pi]$, integrate backwards from $X(\alpha+2\pi)=X(\alpha)$; the same inequality follows because $\sin(\alpha-s)\geq0$ on that second half. Hence every point of the curve lies in the supporting half-plane $x\cdot n(\alpha)\leq h(\alpha)$, and $X(\alpha)$ attains equality. The convex hull of the curve therefore has support function exactly $h$.

For strict inequality in the range, $\rho>0$ and the support-parametrization area formula applies. Orthogonality gives
$$\int_0^{2\pi}h^2=\frac{\pi w^2}{2}+\pi a^2,\qquad \int_0^{2\pi}(h^{\prime})^2=\pi m^2a^2,$$
so $A=\pi w^2/4-\pi(m^2-1)a^2/2$. At either endpoint of the allowed range, replace $a$ by $(1-\varepsilon)a$ and pass to the limit using uniform support convergence and convex-volume continuity. This justifies the formula even where $\rho$ vanishes. Nonzero $a$ does not give a disk, whose support has only a constant term and first harmonics. Evenness gives reflection in the horizontal axis. Choosing uncountably many positive $a$ in the allowed interval even gives distinct areas, hence uncountably many mutually noncongruent examples.

solutions.body_md:
Let $p$ be a corner, with interior angle $\alpha\in(0,\pi)$ and outward normal interval of length $\beta=\pi-\alpha\in(0,\pi)$. For every normal $u$ in this interval, the opposite contact point is $p-wu$ by the binormal identity. These points form a radius-$w$ arc in the boundary. Its endpoints $q,r$ satisfy
$$|q-r|=2w\sin(\beta/2)\leq w.$$
Since $0\leq\beta/2\leq\pi/2$, sine is increasing here, so $\beta\leq\pi/3$ and $\alpha\geq2\pi/3$.

At equality, $p,q,r$ form an equilateral triangle of side $w$. The diameter bound puts $K$ inside $T=B(p,w)\cap B(q,w)\cap B(r,w)$. To recall why $T$ has width $w$, consider its circular boundary arc centered at $p$. At a point $x$ of this arc the outer normal is $u=(x-p)/w$. The opposite supporting point is $p$. Indeed, $z\in T\subset B(q,w)$ gives $2(z-p)\cdot(q-p)\geq|z-p|^2\geq0$, and the disk centered at $r$ gives the same inequality with $r-p$. The vector $u$ is a nonnegative linear combination of $q-p$ and $r-p$, so $(z-p)\cdot u\geq0$ for every $z\in T$. The disk centered at $p$ gives the other supporting line, so the separation is $w$. The same reasoning for all three arcs gives normal intervals of $60^\circ$ each; these intervals and their opposites cover all directions. Thus $T$ has constant width $w$.

Finally $K\subset T$ gives $f(u)=h_T(u)-h_K(u)\geq0$. Equal widths give $f(u)+f(-u)=0$, forcing $f\equiv0$ and hence $K=T$. This last argument is the useful general fact that nested convex bodies of the same constant width must coincide.

solutions.body_md: Write $h(\theta)=w/2+g(\theta)$, where $g(\theta+\pi)=-g(\theta)$. Choose $c\in\mathbb R^2$ to solve $c\cdot n(\theta)=g(\theta)$ and $c\cdot n(\theta+2\pi/3)=g(\theta+2\pi/3)$. The third equality at $\theta+4\pi/3$ holds exactly when $F(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^2g(\theta+2j\pi/3)=0$, since the three normals sum to zero. The continuous function $F$ satisfies $F(\theta+\pi)=-F(\theta)$, hence has a zero. At this angle $h(\theta+2j\pi/3)-c\cdot n(\theta+2j\pi/3)=w/2$ for $j=0,1,2$. Antipodal symmetry gives the same equality at the opposite three normals. These six normals are spaced by $\pi/3$, so the six supporting lines have distance $w/2$ from $c$. Their contact points belong to $K$ and thus satisfy all six half-plane inequalities; consequently each hexagon side really touches $K$. Their intersection is the desired regular hexagon. Its apothem is $w/2$, hence its side length is $w/\sqrt3$ and its area is $\sqrt3w^2/2$. Its vertex-direction width is $2w/\sqrt3$, so it is not a constant-width body.

solutions.body_md: The two copies are full-dimensional convex bodies with disjoint interiors, so a weak separating line exists: for some unit normal $u$ and number $a$, $K_1\subset\{x:x\cdot u\leq a\}$ and $K_2\subset\{x:x\cdot u\geq a\}$. Contact on the line is allowed. In its normal direction their projection intervals have disjoint interiors and both lie in the projection interval of $K$. If the similarity ratios are $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, their widths are $\lambda_1w,\lambda_2w$, independently of rotation. Hence $(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)w\leq w$. Perimeter scales by the similarity ratio, giving the result.

solutions.body_md:
The class is nonempty because it contains the ball of radius $w/2$, and volumes are nonnegative, so choose a sequence whose volumes tend to the infimum. Translate each member $K_n$ to contain the origin; translation preserves both width and volume. Its diameter is $w$, hence $K_n\subset wB$.

Hausdorff selection yields a subsequence converging to a nonempty compact $K\subset wB$. Convexity is preserved under this convergence. The support-distance identity gives uniform convergence $h_{K_n}\to h_K$, so
$$h_K(u)+h_K(-u)=\lim_n\big(h_{K_n}(u)+h_{K_n}(-u)\big)=w$$
for every unit $u$. This limit has nonempty interior: otherwise its affine hull would lie in a proper hyperplane, and a direction orthogonal to that hyperplane would have width zero. Thus $K$ is an admissible width-$w$ convex body. Volume continuity now gives $|K|=\lim_n|K_n|$, equal to the infimum. The translation step is essential to obtain a bounded family before applying compactness.

The support inequalities therefore sandwich the body between $(w-R)B$ and $RB$, proving the inclusion. solutions.body_md:
Maximizing first over unit directions yields $F(c)=\max_u(h_K(u)-c\cdot u)$. The antipodal support identity transforms this into
$$F(c)=w+\max_u(c\cdot u-h_K(u)).$$
If $c\notin K$, the maximum on the right is $\operatorname{dist}(c,K)$. Indeed, every term is at most that distance, and equality holds for the outward direction from the nearest point of $K$ to $c$, whose perpendicular hyperplane supports $K$. If $c\in K$, the minimum of $h_K(u)-c\cdot u$ is the radius of the largest ball centered at $c$ contained in $K$, namely $\operatorname{dist}(c,\partial K)$. This gives the other branch, including zero boundary distance. Both distance terms are strictly positive away from the boundary in their respective regions.

solutions.body_md:
The condition $K\subset B(c,R)$ is equivalent to $h_K(u)-c\cdot u\leq R$ for all unit $u$. Replacing $u$ by $-u$ and using $h_K(-u)=w-h_K(u)$ rewrites it as
$$c\cdot u\leq h_K(u)+R-w\quad\hbox{for every }u.$$
For $R\leq w$ these are exactly the inequalities $c+(w-R)B\subset K$, defining the erosion. For $R\geq w$ the right-hand side is the support function of $K+(R-w)B$, defining that outer parallel body. At $R=w$ the inequalities define $K$ itself. This identifies a locus of centers, not the union of all covering balls.
